segments.text: We'll be live now. So we are on Local Government Port
Companies Accountability Amendments Bill.
So we got the first 15 minutes for the hearing,
the member who carried the bill, Lamanga Solisi.
Do we have her here?
Yeah.
And
I guess you know the rules pretty well. You got 15 minutes.
It would be great if you can leave one or two minutes for the members-
Sure
... of the committee to ask question. And now the floor is yours.
I'll just start my timer, Mr. Chair.
Yes.
Oh.
Well, thank you, Mr. Chair, and members of the Transport and
Infrastructure Select Committee for the opportunity to speak to my member's
bill.
New Zealand has a proud ports and harbors history.
The earliest ports were a little more than a few planks leading into the sea.
20th century industrialization has made wharves an impressive
landscape of soaring cranes and multicolored containers.
But harbor board politics also had a fiery history as central government
established the Chief Marine Board looking after lighthouses, and local government
ran trading ports. New settlers were workforce at outports, and town
folk from local towns wanted more of a say in development and growth,
and sometimes with fiery debates.
But ports were impermanent, temporary short-lived due to key
characteristics of instability, rudimentary facilities,
environment, and economic challenges.
And I tell that story because that's port history in Aotearoa, New Zealand, mid
This bill is an amendment bill. Because it
is a bill that makes sense. And in the first reading, I want to acknowledge
all the members who participated in the first reading to this stage.
I've been asked to explain the problem definition.
What is that bill aiming to fix? Why has this bill been placed in the
member's bill process? And I would like to take this time to take you
through that now.
The bill is a short bill, as members of the select committee have read.
The aim of the bill is to bring transparency and
accountability rules into line with Local Government principles.
Public transparency and accountability and awareness of the
New Zealand public is important for New Zealand consumers and
businesses.
And as the committee is aware, New Zealand relies entirely
on sea freight for survival, yet there is no
national strategy or ports plan.
New Zealand does not have a state-owned or dedicated national
merchant shipping fleet for international trade.
Our international trade is handled by global
shipping,
because deregulation in the late 1980s led to the demise
of major local carriers.
The government has an unbalanced funding model.
Domestic coastal shipping receives zero transport budget,
while road freight receives billions.
Through this funding model, cargo is forced onto local and
nationwide roads, causing congestion and safety
risks and pushing our emissions higher.
Foreign ships carry most of domestic sea freight, completely
exempt of New Zealand taxes, environmental emission laws,
or workers' fair bargaining wage requirements.
And because of that, global conflicts, pandemics, and trade disputes
have a direct impact on these foreign ships.
For example, the fuel crisis and with impact on vessels that
have to come to New Zealand, and that impact may cause
industries to shut down.
This bill reverses the exclusion of port companies and their
subsidiaries from certain rules that apply to council controlled
organizations in the Local Government Act 2002.
This will have the effect of applying normal public accountabilities to
port companies, including the application of the Local
Government Official Information and Meetings Act
1987, the requirement to act as a good
employer, and the requirement to exhibit a sense of
social and environmental
responsibility by having regard to the interests of the
communities in which they operate.
And Mr. Chair, I would like to thank all the submitters who supported this
bill. There were certain themes that came through the submissions, and I
want to use some of those quotations.
Public accountability. The general feeling from submissions
from port companies was there was adequate mechanisms for
public reporting and accountability to enable members
of the public to set their activities, their
strategies, their investments, and so forth,
alongside appropriate protections for commercially
sensitive information
On the contrary, many other submitters welcome the call for
more transparency and easier access to
information concerning the operations and governance
of port companies as a public right,
while at the same time protecting commercial interests that benefit
the public.
Collectively however, the majority of submissions from individuals,
from unions, iwi, hapū, and businesses,
supported the call for increased transparency and public
accountability, and I'm just going to quote a few.
"The Port CEO Group acknowledges and supports the
importance of strong public accountability for port
companies." That was from the Port CEO Group.
"This bill recognizes that ports are not merely commercial
enterprises, but publicly owned institutions whose
decisions have broad public consequences." And that was from the
Rail and Maritime Transport Union.
And from Ms. Bush, "Ports manage public assets worth
billions of dollars. Their decisions affect regional
economies, supply chains, and employment.
Large capital projects carry high financial and operational
risk. Without transparency, boards and councils
cannot make informed decisions."
Another theme, good employer, social and environmental
responsibility. And I'm grateful that many submitters
commented positively about explicit
inclusion of these requirements in the bill. From Ms.
Quinn, "Port companies should be subject to the Local Government
Official Information and Meetings Act 1987,
and the requirements to act as a good employer exhibit a sense of
social and environmental responsibility by having
regard to the interests of the community in which they operate."
That is found in the Local Government Act 2002.
From AJ Marshall, "Ports should be held accountable for
their actions and practices. They are not above or separate from the
law, and the lives and the rights of their workers, tenants, and
visitors deserve to be acknowledged in the legal
process." We also heard from Forest Owners
Association, "We support the bill sets the
expectation that port companies have regard to objectives
beyond profit. While this was not greatly increased legal
constraints on port companies, it sets a norm of
social responsibility and good business practice expected
from companies that are all majority owned and some wholly
owned by local authorities."
From Rail and Maritime Union, "Decisions concerning port
investment, land use, safety, employment, and operations
have significant economic, environmental, and social
consequences, and such decisions should be subject
to public scrutiny." A further theme in
submission was from local iwi with regards to
relationship and restoration. That public
accountability, good employer, social and environmental
responsibility are all elements of the bill that were
interpreted by several submitters as potential
opportunities for restoration and
better future gains.
From Ms. Rollo, "As Māori, I stand in strong support of the
Local Government Port Companies Accountability Amendment
Bill.
For too long, publicly owned port companies have used their legal
exemption from transparency laws to operate as
secretive, profit-driven corporates, completely ignoring
their social, their cultural, and environmental
impacts on local communities and tangata whenua.
First, this bill gives iwi and hapū a critical legal tool to
protect our moana and kaimoana beds.
Port activities such as major harbor dredging, construction, and
industrial runoff happen directly within our
customary and ancestral waters."
The Pirira Coal Tribal Authority submission, they
requested that the committee note the particular significance of this
bill for tangata whenua exercising
kaitiakitanga over waterways and coastal environments
affected by port operations, and that the explanatory
note or parliamentary record explicitly
acknowledge this dimension.
Mr. Chair, there are different approaches and proposed
alternative and amendments that select committee will
consider and decide upon. The key point of
difference between submitters was not the intent of the bill, for example,
better transparency, public accountability, good
employer, social and environment responsibility, but
whether the pathway proposed was the best way to achieve it.
Several submissions, including the New Zealand Law Society, Te Kāhui
Ture o Aotearoa, the Port CEO Group, the
Rail and Maritime Transport Union, discuss the
current legal objective of port companies in Section
5 of the Port Companies Act 1988, which
states,
"The principal objective of every port company shall be
to operate as a successful business." However,
the urgency for success without adequate transparency and
accountability brought risks according to one submitter, who
stated Protect ports from political
interference that prioritises short-term returns
over long-term infrastructure resilience.
And this submitter stated, "The lack of accountability that
leads to waste, inefficiency, and unsafe
practices. Ports should not be allowed to hide failures,
manipulate reporting, or misleading shareholders and
the public." And that was from Ms Bush, who is an
ex-employee of Ports of Auckland.
There were a few proposed alternatives that have already been written
in the public submissions, and so I won't go through that, but I do want to
mention just a quick couple as I wrap up.
The Law Society suggested amendments to PCA and Local
Government, and if required, the Ombudsman Act, rather
than amendments to the Local Government.
And for example, was to amend
Section
5 of the LCA to insert any additional principal
objectives of port companies, and that's already listed in
their written submission.
And Forest Owners Association
supported greater transparency of port company pricing
practices via Local Government and the expectations that
companies have regard to objectives beyond profit, and we heard
that of the submission last week.
Just as I wrap up, the port strategy is so strategically significant,
a type of collaboration that would further encourage closer scrutiny
from, and better collaboration between councils on shared cultural,
social, economic, and environmental interests and goals.
And there were some quotes that were provided already by MUNZ submission.
And so lastly, I do want to thank the Select Committee for
hearing my verbal submission, but also, Mr.
Chair and members, to the CEOs of the port companies
that welcomed me to their
sites and provided some really good intel.
So thank you. I'm happy to take questions.
Great. Simon, and then Dean.
Oh, thank you.
Thank you, and thank you for the explanation.
Compete with other CCOs, as far as I'm

But isn't... Sorry, Simon.

Yes. However, how do you achieve greater
transparency if it is not
mandated under legislation?
All right, Simon. I should come back-
Question is really for you.
Sorry, Simon ... as sponsor of the bill.
Thank you. Yeah.
Not for me, Simon.
Not for the committee.
All right.
Thank you, Simon.

So thank you for your attendance.

I guess

main owners, which is the governing body?
Just throwing out some ideas

One is
whether there should be council appointees on port companies.
Two is whether ports should be more accountable
to their owners. For example, being
required to appear before governing bodies
on an annual basis, much like select committees do with

I guess, I'm curious as to whether you've considered
other such mechanisms,
rather than
just the local process, because I think there's been some serious
concerns raised around that, so I'm just keen to get your thoughts on that.
Appreciate the question.
There have been further considerations as to what is the best
legislative tool to achieve the objectives.
Certainly, my visits to the ports,
with the respective CEOs of the different port companies, shared
their
personal views as to why they did not
support this bill and their concerns
around publicly listed companies, for example.
I have looked at a few other, what is the effective tool by
way of public accountability or transparency?
Many of the CEOs, and I think I visited seven of the port
companies, including the three biggest.
Oh, sorry, not Littleton, but certainly Auckland, Tauranga.
And those CEOs shared that they did not support the
legislation because according to them, this was the tool, the
current under Port Companies Act was the best tool.
So I questioned them as to what about the accountability and
transparency, given the fact that there is no...
I don't know if there's other work happening on a nationwide port strategy.
You've heard that some of the unions have got concerns in terms of the workers.
But certainly with iwi and other individuals like local businesses,
we're asking them what is the best tool to get greater
transparency and accountability in their view.
So hence some were supporting.
Yeah.
Some did raise concern in terms of submitters.
Yes.
That probably might-
Yeah, no worries. Just one more supplementary if I can is, have you-- I know
you have a government experience at the local level yourself, but
have you engaged with councilors and local authorities
over this issue to understand what their needs are?
Because they are elected by the people.
These assets are held on,
really in ownership of local authorities.
So I'm keen to get a sense of what feedback you're getting from
local elected leaders on their needs in terms
of what they think may drive transparency and accountability.
Not as many as I would have liked to, given the time constraint.
However, there were a couple in support of better
transparency under their local government in
terms of Auckland Council, which is quite different.
Probably spoke to only one council from the Tauranga area.
Okay. Oh, well, thank you, member. The times is up.
Once again, thank you so much for your presentation.
Thank you.

Pirirākau Tribal Authority Incorporated.
I appear for Pirirākau Hapū, mana whenua o Ngāhi Ka, whose rohe
encompasses the western Tauranga harbor catchments and Te
Awanui. Our status is legislated
under the Ngā Hapu o Ngāti Ranginui Claims Settlement Act
Pirirākau strongly supports this bill.
This bill targets a structural deficit.
Port companies are majority-owned by regional councils through
council-controlled holding companies.
Port of Tauranga Limited, for example, is 54%
owned by Quayside Holdings, the investment arm of Bay
of Plenty Regional Council. And this isn't a unique situation to
Tauranga. Napier Port, South Port at Bluff, and Marsden
Maritime at Northport all share the same structure.
Majority council-owned, NZX-listed,
and equally exempt from the accountability frameworks their parent
councils must meet.
Yet despite that dominant public ownership, port
companies have been carved out from the transparency standards that
apply to other publicly controlled entities.
That carve out is the anomaly this bill is correcting.
Our insistence on this is driven by direct experience.
Pirirākau is currently engaged in the FastTrack Approvals
Act process for the Port of Tauranga's Stellar Passage development,
large-scale dredging and wharf extensions within Te Awanui, Tauranga
Harbor. That process exposed an accountability
void. Outside of high-stakes capital applicants,
there is zero enforceable mechanisms to access background data
to fit the port's commercial footprint.
But Te Awanui is a single interconnected system.
Sediment and tidal flows do not stop at the edge of a
corporate lease.
This bill closes three specific gaps.
First, Section 74,
port companies are currently immune to official information requests under
LGOIMA. That's indefensible for entities operating
under majority council ownership within public
waterways.
LGOIMA access would let us request monitoring data, ecological
assessments, and operational records relevant to
kaitiakitanga.
That is a specific documented need, not a hypothetical one.
Second, Section 60A, this stops port companies from
locking in major decisions behind closed doors, then presenting
communities with the paperwork to rubber stamp it.
Third, Section 59, this provides a statutory framework
to challenge the artificial separation between port
operations and their environmental consequences.
Now, I wanted to talk and to address specifically the commercial
risk argument directly. This bill, in our
view, does not alter commercial mandates.
LGOIMA already contains robust protections for
genuinely commercially sensitive information.
Those
protections are tested and well understood.
If a majority council-owned port can only
compete by operating with less transparency than
other publicly controlled entities, it's confessing its business
model relies on hiding its true cost from the public.
Pirirakau recommends the passing of this bill in its current form,
tightened subsidiary coverage to capture all joint ventures and
secondary structures, and extended coverage to Section
57 for mandatory community consultation on
long-term strategic plans. Port companies
operate in public waterways, on publicly owned land,
under majority public ownership.
This exemption has no principal justification in our view,
and its consequences fall disproportionately on those of us
who live with the environmental and cultural effects of port
operations daily.
For Pirirakau, this is not abstract.
It manifests as information asymmetry, accountability
gaps- ... and structural barriers to kaitiakitanga.
This bill addresses those consequences directly and
proportionately without disrupting commercial
operations. Tēnā koutou. Happy to take questions.

amendment,

key renewal

information, creates no council veto, and leaves the
decision with the port board.
It is a narrow safeguard for very large
long-term decisions. I ask the committee to seek
advice on it. Thank you.
